review_text: Perched majestically atop Swami Rock in Trincomalee, the Thirukoneswaram Kovil is one of Sri Lanka’s most sacred Hindu sites. Dedicated to Lord Shiva, this ancient "Temple of a Thousand Pillars" is one of the five historical Pancha Ishwarams built to protect the island. The temple is famous for its vibrant Dravidian architecture and the massive, golden seated Shiva statue that overlooks the Indian Ocean. Visitors are drawn to the breathtaking "Lovers’ Leap" cliff, offering panoramic sea views. Despite facing destruction in the 17th century, the temple remains a powerful symbol of resilience and spiritual devotion, blending deep history with stunning natural beauty.

I visited Thirukoneswaram Kovil in Trincomalee last week, and once again it reminded me why this temple is so special. This was my third visit, and every time I come here, the experience feels new, peaceful, and deeply spiritual. The moment you step inside the kovil, you can feel the calmness. The sea breeze, the ancient architecture, and the powerful energy of the place make your mind completely relaxed. The view from the top is truly breathtaking — the blue ocean stretching far beyond your eyes. It feels like nature itself is giving you a blessing. The temple premises are well maintained and very clean. Watching people pray with devotion, hearing the bells, and standing in front of Lord Shiva’s sanctum gives a beautiful sense of peace. Every visit makes me feel more connected to my faith and culture. If you are visiting Trincomalee, Thirukoneswaram Kovil is a must-visit, not just for religious reasons but also for the history, beauty, and the peaceful atmosphere it offers. I know this won’t be my last visit — this temple always pulls me back with its divine charm.

Once in the parking lot, in the midst of the deer and peacocks, you cross an alley lined with shops and the temple is there, just upstairs.You have to put on your shoes (on a hot temple, provide socks so as not to burn your feet while walking). No admission fee, you make a free donation when you get your shoes back. The temple had an important destiny during the 1st millennium AD. Dating back to BC, successive kings gave it scope and fame. At the beginning of the 17th century, fearing a Portuguese invasion, the religious and notables of Trincomalee threw into the sea, just below the cliff on which the temple is erected, the important pieces to escape the invader. They were attacked: in 1623, the Portuguese took the city and razed the temple. It was not until 1950 that divers (including science fiction writer Arthur Clarke) rediscovered these submerged remains. The coins are reassembled and used to reconstruct the current temple, associated with more recent elements. Some of the pieces have remained underwater, just above the cliff, and are an extraordinary diving spot. Koneswaram means "where Shiva is". A grand Shiva status is at the entrance to the temple. The interior consists of mystical scenes and religious effigies. Just at the entrance to the cliffside path, a tree collects wooden crates that the faithful hang on its branches. These are symbolized cradles, with the tree receiving prayers related to fertility requests.

Koneswaram Temple of Trincomalee (Tamil: திருக்கோணேச்சரம் கோயில்) or Thirukonamalai Konesar Temple – The Temple of the Thousand Pillars and Dakshina-Then Kailasam (Southern / Ancient Kailash) is a classical-medieval Hindu temple complex in Trincomalee, a Hindu religious pilgrimage centre in Eastern Province, Sri Lanka. The most sacred of the Pancha Ishwarams of Sri Lanka, it was built significantly during the ancient period on top of Konesar Malai, a promontory overlooking Trincomalee District, Gokarna bay and the Indian Ocean. The monument contains its main shrine to Shiva in the form Kona-Ishvara, shortened to Konesar.

Upon entering, you are overwhelmed with a huge statue of the Hindu Lord Shiva. This one is pink, it baffles me how many different interpretations there are of Shiva? Anyway to the left of him nestled beneath a tree are several deer. They graze on the grass and birds are also amongst them squawking happily. The usual traditional temple surroundings are here. After two weeks in Sri Lanka, it’s all too familiar and nothing more than decoration over slabs of concrete. Elaborate in parts whist needing some tlc in other parts. The incense burns, the chanting is soft and tourists are both fascinated and more than happy to emulate the rituals of locals. For me personally I was more impressed with its location. At the edge of a steep mountain rock offering panoramic views of a beach and the sea. You could hear waves gently crash and take in the fresh air. It’s a popular destination if you’re spiritual or take it with a pinch of salt. Either way, it’s well worth a visit for the scenery alone. It’s also free entry, which makes you wonder why in other temples they charge an extortionate rate entrance fees.

Surrounded by the dramatic Swami Rock and Gokarna Bay, the classical-medieval complex is Trinco’s biggest draw. The site is a major Hindu pilgrimage center, and one of the Pancha Ishwarams (five abodes of Shiva) built in Sri Lanka to honor one of the principle deities of Hinduism. This temple is situated in the village of Thambalagamuwa that was part of the medieval semi-independent feudal division called Thambalagamuwa Pattu. Prior to the arrival of Portuguese in 1622 and then Dutch colonial overloads in 1656, leaders of the Thambalagamuwa Pattu and others around it were independent rulers sometimes subject to Jaffna kingdom or Kandyan kingdom.

The biggest tourist attraction is Koneswaram Temple, on a high clifftop overlooking the ocean. The fort remains and is now a military base, but the temple has been rebuilt and the site's antiquity attracts many pilgrims.

We visited this famous Koneswaran Temple situated on Swamy Rock within Fort Fredrick on 5th May 2018.  The vehicle park is about 150 metres from the temple itself. A little beyond the temple entrance the view outside into the sea is beautiful, with many fishing boats.  The sheer drop at one of these places is called the “lover’s leap” where a distraught lady flung herself to the watery grave after watching her lover, a member of the Dutch foreign service, sailing away back to Holland. What struck me most were the little colourful baskets, said to be small versions of baby cots, hanging on one of the trees towards the sea side under flags of various colours.  These are offerings from childless couples asking for divine intervention for them to have their baby. We spent a thoroughly enjoyable morning visiting this beautiful and historic location.

Visiting the Siva Ishwarams (Pancha Ishwarams) in Sri Lanka. The reunion with relatives in Jaffna took us to four of the Siva Temples in Sri Lanka during the first seven days of our Sri Lanka Odyssey. Our first stop, on March 3rd, was at the Munneswaram temple situated in a village in the Puttalam District. Hindus believe that it is one of the the five temples they need to visit in their life time. The others being Naguleswaram temple which we visited in Keerimalai in the Kankesanthurai district on March 4th and Thiruketheeshwaram in Mannar District and the Koneswaram temple in Trincomalee (Thirukonamalai) -- both the next day. All these, including Rameswaram in India form the five ancient temples (Ishwarams) dedicated to Shiva. According to Hindus, the Munneswaram temple near Puttalam is the temple where King Rama prayed to Shiva after killing Ravana to seek forgiveness over the death of many in the war. Hindus believe that the Naguleswaram temple's adjacent water tank, the Keerimalai Springs, has curative properties. The temple was largely destroyed by Jesuit missionaries following the Portuguese conquest of the Jaffna kingdom, restored by Arumuga Navallar in 1894. The Thiruketheeshwaram temple had existed for more than 2,400 years. During our visit to this temple, we witnessed a temple devotee from Vavunia singing Thevarams. His aim was to complete the 800 thurmurai thevarams in one month. The Trincomelee Koneswaram temple was built by the Cholas/Pandian kings. The temple is situated atop Konesar Malai, at a commanding position overlooking the Indian Ocean. It is also known as the "Mount Kailash of the South". The temple, mentioned in Mahabaratha and Ramayana, was visited by Arunagirinathar and is the easternmost shrine of the five ancient Ishwarams of Shiva on the island.

The Most Sacred Śrī Śānkarī Dévi Temple (Thiru Konéśwaran Koil) complex is located within the sprawling old Portuguese Fort. From the parking lot there is a 10-minute–walk up to the Temple. Among the several foreign visitors we met German, Spanish, Italian, Scottish and Chinese tourists. That shows the popularity of this place. Laxmi’s long-term wish got fulfilled this evening after we were blessed with a very happy and blissful Divine Sight of Śrī Śānkarī Dévi and Her Lord Śrī Śiva in this only Śakti Peeţhaṃ in Sri Lanka – known locally as Konéśwara Ālayaṃ – Śrī Mahā Śakti Peeţhaṃ Temple - of the eighteen (the remaining seventeen being located in India) at this MOST SACRED PLACE in Trincomalee. The surrounding views are full of greenery and so beautiful. The blue Indian Ocean appearing on both sides of the Temple Complex presented a lovely spectacle! The Scottish couple took me to be a Guide and said they were not going to pay me anything when I volunteered to explain the story of Śrī Mārkaṇḑéya in the complex. However, they were very happy to listen to the Purāṇic legend narrated by me - about Sage Mārkaṇḑéya as even the God of Death Yama had to take off his crown and mace and surrender totally before Lord Siva when commanded by Siva to spare the life of His devotee Mārkaṇḑéya!  They profusely thanked me after hearing my narration and felt so happy knowing that I was a student at the Imperial College, London, long time ago but  that I was not a Guide! The Scotsman respectfully took off his hat and bowed before Lord Śiva in reverence. It was learnt that the Portuguese who were in occupation of Sri Lanka in the 16 Century AD destroyed the original Temple and threw all the magnificent sculptured stone columns down into the sea below. Three bronze statues were lately brought up by divers, found among the columns buried in the sea, one of which has been mounted atop the hill facing the entrance to the renovated Temple. The Temple opened at 5 O’Clock in the evening. The Tamil priests first performed the prescribed customary rituals to the Lord. We have then made our own humble offerings to the Presiding Deity Śrī Śānkarī Dévi. We had the Most Divine Sight and blessings of the Holy Lord and His Divine Consort while witnessing in awe all the Pūja Worships done by the Tamil priests in the huge, peaceful and Serene complex.
I took great pictures (for once) and I wish I could post them but I changed my cell phone. Anyways, the place is beautiful and very relaxing ! I recommend this place if you go to sri lanka.

We visited this famous temple and were impressed with all aspects. The location of the temple on a hill overlooking the sea made for great setting. The priest's prayers were soothing to listen to and we felt the presence of God. The link with Ravana and Ramayan showed the closeness of Sri Lankan culture to Indian culture. All in all, a visit to remember!
Best place in Sri Lanka 🇱🇰✌🏽visit this if your in trincomalee for many years this god has given blessings to all our country

We went up to the temple but was not permitted to drive up all the way up the hill to the temple as there was a problem with the historic arch leading up to the temple. The temple and it architecture was beautiful and it s location on the hilltop overlooking the bay was beyond description.The view from the temple across the bay was fantastic. We even sighted a peacock in the vicinity of the temple in the bushes surrounding the temple hill side.We spent about twenty minutes in the temple and having prayed left and walked back. As you cant wear your shoes into the temple, there is a small stall on the left hand side as you near the temple where you can leave your shoes for a small token sum. All of you in the group can put your shoes/ sandals or slippers in one compartment. A number of the closet holding your shoes will be given to you to collect them on your return. the temple is worth a visit as it is of historical interest.

Lovely hindou temple, stunning view on Trinco bay, amazing gods sculptures, one of our favorite temple during our trip! Inside and out, just enjoy all the serenity and spirituality around, don't need to be a beliver to fell that this place is one of the peacfull you're never been :)
Hindu devotees must visit this temple and one of four lingas established by lord Rama. Other story is temple is built by Ravana
nothing much to say, it's good place to visit. and have to buy many fancy items tto bring to home. and can see lovers lip
It is something local and cultural. Not touristic. Be there when Pooja happens. You will see lot of local devotees and their culture.

This location is at the tip of the land at a high point and as such offers great views. It has a rich Hindu legend and so my parents were keen to visit it. You need to reach the naval base and from there, the only way up is a tuk-tuk (auto-rickshaw in Indian). Very elaborate art on the walls depicting a lot of history. We also bought some local sweet-meats on our way back and they were delicious!

We reached the temple in the morning and had a good darshan. This temple is close to the shore. You will be able to see the sea from the top of the temple. The temple follows rituals as in Tamil Nadu. Once you enter the temple, you have the presiding deity of  lord shiva. You can easily spend 30 to 45 minutes in this temple. This is MUST visit temple in Sri Lanka.
The place where temple is located is very beautiful, specially in evening. Historical background also nice. can see the bay and trincomalee city nicely.
This is a beautiful temple , breathtaking and enormous. We had a lovely trip from Uppuvelie in a three wheeler.  On the way we stoped to see

It was a beautiful temple located on top on the hill overlooking the indian ocean. We bought pooja tray from one of the stalls for reasonable price to experience the rituals and must say it was simple and tourist friendly. The priest was helpful and friendly, The pooja started on time and it was simple and short pooja. Thank you temple management for giving us this beautiful experience.
Rich in history, mystery and great people. The small walk towards Koneswaram is very interesting with handmade crafts and little toys for kids.

If you are into temples then worth a look because its built on the hill and the scenery is worth the trip ,you will have to go through the local market place to get their, as usual the markets are full of local produce all very snuggery so be aware you diabetics , and pick the stall that has a cover over the food because the place can be full of flies , do keep your hand bags secured or the monkeys will have a field day pulling things out that you do not want anyone to see. I am not into pagan worship mind you we do have a lot of pagans ruling our world at present.

This would be one o the things to do ar Trincomale apart from enjoying the beach. The temple is up a hill and quite a walk from the bus station so preferably take a tuk-tuk uphill. The temple is nothing great but does give you great views of Trinco. There are any small shops lining the temple. On your way back walk downhill which is pretty pleasant and worth the effort.

I went there with lot of expectations after reading the reviews, especially of the views from the top, since this temple is located up a small hill. Tuk Tuk will charge your 150 LKR from the bus stand. Fredrick. I reached there only by 6 p.m. Hence did not look at the fort and went up the hill to the temple. You will have to walk the last 50 yards to the temple. There is a place where you can leave your footwear. The views of the sea and other places is good but you do not get a direct unhindered view. Very nice place of ancient Hindu temple God  as Koneshwar. Surrounded by sea with natural forest. Peacock, deer, monkey are friendly moving here and there. Mind blowing as well as smoothing the mind if we there.

Wonderfully peaceful and beautiful retreat with a most imposing image of Khali as you arrive.  Take some smaller notes for buying offerings (as stallholders will tell you that they can’t change larger notes – this happens a lot in Sri Lanka, be prepared).  Women will need to take something to cover legs and shoulders and shoes/sandals left at the approach. Make sure that you see the deer too, there are a lot of them!
This Indu temple is simply amazing with a wonderful view on the sea! Absolutely worth going! Dont miss it!

The level of details in this Hindu temple was impressive. We unfortunately missed the pooja (prayer). You should plan to be there at the right time, so you get the full experience. 30-45 min drive from Trinco city.

If in the area, you must come and see this holy temple. it is ornate and pretty. It does get hot, and although there is some carpeting your feet will still get hot. There are plenty of stalls on the walk up, and you are also passing through the old portuguese fort, now home to the SL army. Odd to think that only 9 years ago this area was part of the civil war, but now so peaceful.

This Ancient Temple located on a rocky outcrop overlooking the ocean is a must for all visitors to Sri lanka.  Sacred to Hindus , is also full of history and hindu culture.   A lot to see and absorb in the design and architecture of the temple.    Modest dress and no footwear

If you visit the Koneswaram temple you will see many of the most famous places in Sri Lanka. You have to go through the Fort Frederick which was built by Portugese during the time they invaded Sri Lanka on your way to the temple. This tour through take you back through the ages to the colonial times. One past the Fort buildings you have to walk up to the temple. It is Advisable to go there before 10,00 AM or after around 4.00 PM because the ground could be really hot and you have to walk bare foot. There are many impressive statues of Hindu gods in the temple. Within the temple premises is the famous 'lovers leap' a picturesque sight. On your way back visit the War Museum where you could see parts of ships built in 18 hundred as well as the weapons captured from the guerilla outfits LTTE and JVP. It is also an educational tour. If you go on a Sunday stroll down the Trincomalee city. I stayed at Sober Island Resort which is a good place to stay. Its a resort inside a sort of a jungle but you have to be recommended by a person in the SL Navy to book the resort.
Having dived below the temple, it was interesting to visit and see the various icons inside the temple. Well worth a visit.

Avoid going between 1 & 4 when there is no darshan. The view of the ocean is amazing from the staircase that goes down right across the main door of the temple. Best view of the ocean I have had in a decade.

Nice setting on a cliff  high above the sea. Mainly frequented by local Hindus who can purchase in one of the stalls along the road leading up to the temple. Some tourists also stop here on their way to a beach resort. On hot days the ground can burn your feet outside the temple so you might want bring socks...
Go for the views and look at the colonial buildings and grounds of the fort. Don't forget to have shoulders and knees covered. The ground from where you leave your shoes to the temple was scalding.

it was nice to visit a hindu temple, yet if there has some English descriptions, it should be nicer! got a bonus checkpoint before leaving which was a budda parade. p.s. shoes off and about 100m walk, beware of the wet ground

Unseasonal rains started up just as we arrived which added to the atmosphere. The open design meant that everyone was confined to one side of the temple to shelter from the rain. So I'd try time a visit for just before a service, we were there at 4pm, there is maybe 3 in the morning and 3 in the evening. Temple could close in the afternoon I'm not sure. I had seen a lot of Buddha buildings, so this was the first time I saw something of the Hindu religion! Very nice and beautiful, if you are in Trincomolee, please visit this place!
Best view of Trincomalee and the Temple is very impressive Colorfull with a lots of paintings, statues and sculptures: we loved this place!

What a colourful and nice temple this is in Trincomalee. Outside there is a large statue of the Godess Shiva which is impressive. Inside there are lots of colourful statues to see; we were lucky as a ceremony just started when we arrived. Be aware, at an Hindu temple women need to wear a sarong and you have to enter without shoes.

Full of locals, with the real atmosphere of a saint place. There are great views from above all the city and harbour. We took the tuk-tuk up the hill (it's quite fat from the city center) and made a deal with a driver to wait for us. It took about half an hour to see all the place. Take socks with you! The path is really hot  and you are obliged to leave the shoes at the entrance (for free, but we packed ours to the bag and took with us).

Ancient Shiva Temple on the cliff. Closely attached to King Ravana. The story of the temple was superb. The view on all the sides were breath taking. Well maintained temple. Family can spend sometime on the top enjoying the views.
This is a good trip to provide some variety from lying on the beach. There are great views from the bay from the top. I would recommend getting a tuk tuk up and walking back down.
The temple excursion itself was an average experience. The surrounding views though offered some lovely photo opportunities.

Although it is one of the must see sites in eastern Sri Lanka, one must be mindful that it is a sacred religious venue which should be treated like that. I always found it extremely refreshing to walk to the temple early in the mornings enjoying the unique experience of first strolling along one of the most beautiful beaches in the country and then to enter the monumental fort Frederick and walk uphill among herds of deer which is one of the most unique and fantastic experiences one could have. The temple itself is majestic and one can learn a lot about its history and interesting stories of Hindu gods if accompanied by a knowledgeable Hindu devotee. Not being a Hindu myself, I always enjoyed and admired the traditional early morning rituals that take place. Last but not the least, the view of the city, fishing harbour, the open ocean, and down 'lovers leap' from up there is incomparable.
Located on a perfect sight with breathtaking scenic sea view, ideal time to visit early morning or evening!
A gorgeous and beautifully located temple full of friendly worshippers. Colourful and glorious. An easy walk. The sweet looking cow outside the temple is actually an attack cow... beware!
On the top of the rock through the dutch fort. You can see the far waters of east beach from the top. Nice location

This temple is beautiful and it's free. You can see the locals pray and catch a great view of Trinco. Women should cover shoulders and legs. They do have covers available at the entry. We were pleasantly surprised by how much we enjoyed this.

Nothing else remarkable to say about this site. Lots of deer were seen. Lots of local sweet delicacies to buy. Have to take of shoes to store at LKR20 per cubby hole. Very hot day so could not stay long.
Grate Hindu Temple. Best time to visit early in the morning. Lot of visitors from all over the world visit this temple.

Seeing the temple was an interesting experience. Please remember that if there are people who are not able to walk a long distance, they can go in a vehicle all the way up to the temple. There is a sign that says no vehicles are allowed but there are exceptions.

It's a wonderful and Historic place, large statue inside. This is a hindu's religious place. One has to experience the sea breeze.

I've seen a few temples and sacred places, but I did not like this one at all. I don't understand all the positive reviews... The location of the temple makes it all the more beautiful. We visited the temple when a local ritual was on and the sound of the drums was mesmerizing.
A very  religious place where people from all religions visit when in Trincomalee.and a very religious place and as a Very long history.it's Location is fantastic

This is an amazing Temple with many legendary stories about its history and rituals carried out by its religious pilgrims who visit. It is recommended that you have a tour guide who is of the same faith or well versed in its history.
Visit this temple when a mass is going on! It´s an expierience you will not forget! Really a Must-See in Sri Lanka!

Really colorful and I loved the place. Super view from the temple when you look down towards the sea.
This place has a long history. Sacred place for both Hindus and buddhists. Beautiful sea view. One of the main attractions of trincomalee.

I like temples so this was high on my list.  It sits on the hill at the top of the cliffs at the end of the peninsula with great views.  The temple itself is impressive with fascinating pictures and artefacts.  If you like temples, this is a great visit.
The colors and decoration of this Hindu Temple certainly catch the eye. I would recommend visiting during a service in order to obtain an idea of the ritual and solemnity of the place.

This is a really lovely Hindu Temple in a great setting, up on a hill, right by the ocean.  There are various caves and niches in the rocks that have been used to house some of the Hindu idols / artifacts.

A very colourful Hindu temple set high on the cliff above the sea. Very important Temple for Hindus. Am not a massive fan of temple visits. This ticked a box and would probably tick many for temple aficionados.
this is a huge kovil in trincomalee town. on the way you can see lot of deers. firt time thought they are made of concrete but NOO! get close to see them real.

Before entering you need to take off your shoes and keep in the racks available there. Since the hill is on the edge of the sea, the view of sea from the top is real breath taking. A must see place while you are at Trincomalee.
I´ve visited many temples of a wide variety of religions in many countries. I never saw an advertisment like the one they have in the entrance. It seems they are quite rigid!!
A pretty little temple with outstanding views over the bay , stalls are lining the road up to it with the usual temple tat . Very pleasant .
One of the best sea views you can have in Sri Lanka on top of the rock. Breathtaking. Must visit place in Trinco.
This is a very famous place among all religion. They have magnificent statues. Can see the whole trinco city when you reach there.

You can walk to this place from Trinco town...try it... the view from the top is beautiful.... you can see beautiful seas from here... on the way to the top where you find the Statues u find many street shops where u good buy collectibles.souvenirs, food items etc. Have a visit if u travel to Trinco!
One of the most important and holy Hindu temples in Sri Lanka, open all hours, gives you a good feel of the local Tamil culture.
It was a rainy day hence the temple was almost empty.  Neat and clean environment! Not dress code restrictions!  Loved this place.

This is a very historic temple in Trinco and definitely worth a visit. Its on top of a hill next to the ocean. Its a very touristy place with full of tourists. You need to park the vehicle quite far away and walk up to the temple
It is very nice &beautiful place in sri lanka...visited the temple in evening ,the temple is located at the edge of the  hill which is facing the sea.It is pleasent atmosphere.

This is a place never to be missed any one visiting Trincomalee. Threre are so many stories of this place in the past which cannot be written one by one. I had the opportunity to visit this ancient site after about 35 years and there are lots of changes. In my last visit on 1980's there were no temperary souvenier stalls and the kovil was not this large like now. What I saw was one of the most beautiful places over looking the entrance to the port from the ocean, the natural harbour and the fishing harbour. All could be sighted so well and it was one of the most spectacular senaries. But now there are so many temperary shops as well as the kovil has extended all sorts of buildings at the edge of the rock the spectacular scenary has vanished. Thre are only few accesses to the scenary it is so dissapointing. The authorities have authorised build all the scenery covering buildings it is really really dissapointing. I reckon still its a very good and beutiful place to viisit. One advise read about the history of this place before you visit!

The Koneswaram temple is one of most holy Hindu shrines to the god Shiva in Sri Lanka and is well worth a visit. It is easily approached by car or the ubiquitous tuk tuk readily hired close to most local tourist hotels around Trincomalee town. The high rock on which the temple stands gives great views out to sea and coast. Be aware that the dropping off point is a hundred yards or so from the temple near a range of souvenir stalls. The last part of the approach requires bare feet (this can be a bit hard on the feet) as is usual when visiting shrines and shoes can be deposited in a rack for this purpose. The temple and surrounds are lavishly decorated with colourful statutes and a number of dioramas illustrating stories from the lives of the gods.

Following a gentle walk up to the temple passed a few stalls selling hats and souvenirs we saw the colourful statue with the temple behind. We were privilaged to be allowed to join a ceremony  and (we are female) local females showed us what to do. We bought a ticket at a kiosk to give to the priests to bless us. The temple is beautiful inside but no pictures allowed. Behind the temple were lots of little cradles hung on trees for fretility wishes. Beautiful views out to sea and across the bay. We ended with a cool orange juce in the cafe on the hill where we watched the sun set.
Visited this place on a rainy day. The temple is located right on the edge of a hill facing the Blue Ocean. You get pleasant sightings of deer as well.

We went there during late January and unfortunately it turned out to be a very hot day. You have to leave your transport a fair way from the temple and walk the rest of the distance bare foot. We found it very uncomfortable to walk on the tarmac which was  extremely hot for us. Managed to get as close as you can to get a good view of the temple  but could not venture in.

Went to the temple towards the evening on a special feast day so it was quite busy. Dropped off well before temple since unable to get closer and walked down road through many shops selling everything either side. Ahead was the temple, splendid location on a promontory the cliff edge. Down the side of the cliffs were various statues and places for prayer. Outside the temple we were met by a huge statue and inside was extremely colourful and beautiful and well worth seeing. The only downside was the temple guardian. Some musllim ladies walked in, heads covered. [not allowed] A few words were passed and as they removed their head wear as a mark of respect more words were passed and they were ordered out. Surely in a religious setting  tolerance and empathy would not be amiss. Despite this episode some interesting customs outside, smashing coconuts for fertility..  Back up the road to the shops and to collect ones shoes.

Right on the Indian Ocean, this temple is a relatively new version of an ancient temple that Portuguese invaders destroyed several centuries ago. But Hindu Tamil priests keep the services going, several times a day. This temple was out of bounds for several years during the civil war and is now opening up again as peace returns to Sri Lanka

We are told there are over 1800 steps but they are shallow and should not prove a problem for anyone of average fitness.  More of a challenge is getting to the final high spot over steep, smooth rock with a few footholds, there is a hand rail but you may have to let go to let people down!  You will need a head for heights at the top the barriers are low but the view is stupendous.  There are several other shrines on the way up with their own story and well worth the visit.  For more information visit the web page for the temple.

A nice place to visit especially during the afternoon puja. The temple complex has some interesting sights apart from the main temple. The locals are very friendly and welcoming and they might even invite you to join them in a simple meal after the puja. As with almost all kovils in Sri Lanka, pictures are not allowed inside the main temple but men do not have to take their shirts off. The puja itself is more subdued compared to the ones we have observed in other parts of Sri Lanka.

The Koneswaram Hindu Temple is definitely a 'must see' when in Trincomalee. One has to walk for a few minutes along the road leading to it (with no shoes), then a short climb up into the Temple itself. You pass numerous street vendors selling sweet foods, hats and souvenirs. The Temple itself is a masterpiece of architecture and Hindu decorations and art work. Apart from the glory of the Temple one can enjoy superb panoramic views from the grounds, overlooking the town and distant beaches.

A great place for theologians and others seeking insights on the Ramayana! The place is situated with a great panoramic view of the city and sea! A must for visitors to this city! Dressing must be decent in view of religious sentiments and taboo. The pictures and paintings inside which includes archeological findings really heartwarming and breathtaking! The stalls leading to the temple a great place for souvenirs and fair priced! But please do bargain for a great deal! Do not miss catching a glimpse of the deers!
Walk around a Hindu temple barefoot. Look at the ocean and get a taste of Tamil culture. Just a short walk from the bus station. Not to mention the very tame deer.
Koneswaram Temple is an  Interesting Place to visit and study. A history of decades and we had a wonderful time.
evidence for ramayana in this koneshwaram temple is rawana cut. though you believe or not there is a cut shape in stone. sacred place. nice place. easily can reach from trincomalee town.
This ancient Kovil has a history of being a magnet for childless women. You will see toy cradles hung on a tress by women praying for a child.

There is parking available at this temple free of charge. The walk to the temple is quite short but a little on the hilly side. There are stalls selling offerings to take with you to the temple and also stalls selling drinks and ice-creams. Once you get closer to the temple you have to remove your shoes as usual and pay Rupees 20.00 to reclaim them again. The ground in the afternoon to the temple once you remove your shoes can be rather challenging as it becomes very hot. The temple itself is well worth a visit and the views from the top are truly magnificent. Sadly there are many spotted deer that have taken residency next to the temple, and have begun to beg for food from the devotees. Many people, including ourselves, stop to take photographs of the resident spotted deer. I only hope that people do not get them too familiar with begging for food due to feeding, that they completely forget how to forage for themselves.

Koneswaram temple is a hindu temple an dknown as teh first among the shakti peetams .. very very nice .. well maintained ,clean and perfect place to worship... as the place is visited by many Indians  .. they are accepting Indian currency also....
went and had a look, wasn't planning on it, but we went; had to remove shoes, put on sarong, but no worries. be respectful of people worshiping, and taking photos without asking.

Visited on an early morning excursion with the family. Love the rich colours of this temple and with few people around you got a definite sense of peace and calm which was appreciated. Lots of little nooks and crannies with different deities and enjoyed the views of the Indian Ocean as well. Would definitely recommend any travellers to Trinco to tick this exquisite temple off the list.

A picturesque stroll from the fort that borders the temple allows amazing views back over Dutch bay and Trinco town. There is a number of vendors just before the entrance, selling an array of gifts for the locals. Do yourself a favour and sample some of the sweets, they are delightful. The temple itself is visited by large numbers of locals, making the short walk.
Surrounded by sea with colourful temple. God koneswar one of the ancient temple for Hindus. Very silence and peaceful for mind

This is a beautiful temple with a lot of old artifacts and history dating back to the time of King Ravana. The location is fabulous, with views of the Trincomalee town and the beaches from the temple.

Very crowded, interesting place. You dont see many tourists there. On the way to the temple you can buy tacky, chinese stuff and snacks. The temple is worth to see. Very colorful and the way through the Fort is nice

I spent a few hours up at Koneswaram Temple which is only a five minute bicycle ride from me. It stood here since 400 BC, one of the sacred sites for Hindus, and is mentioned in Mahabharata. I wasn’t looking for the temple, just felt like climbing up above the ocean, but there it was. You will be given a piece of fabric to wrap around your deliciously brown knees if you happen to wear shorts. It is free, give it back on return. You will need to take off your shoes and leave them in the box rack. Walk barefoot on the baking hot slab stones and sand of the main approach. It will make you hop and run into the shade of temple real fast. I loved being up there. It sits atop the Swami rock over the Ocean into the vertigenous cliffs, the crows fly between the columns, there is an air of gentle decay, abandonment and a spirit of generations who lived, believed, perished; nothing, but a fairytale left. The breeze from the ocean sings in the ears, and a giant statue of Golden Shiva gazes past you into the distance of the harbour. So peaceful, no crowds, no tourists. I shudder to think about this becoming like the Pyramids. When I saw those at 25, I wanted to cry.. from a shrill sense of impossibility to be one to one with eternity… bloody crowds, and sure I was one of them too. A Temple worker perceptively told me ‘You love it here, don’t you.. come any time’. The devastating beauty of the location and a strange air of dignity that the human touch afforded it.. when you see both the military ship patrolling the harbour AND a giant turtoise splashing at the surface.. just fills one with gratitude for being part of it all… in this needle of space and time. I could die there tomorrow, and that would be OK.

The original temple of a thousand pillars that stood here was destroyed by the Portuguese in 1624 and the stones used to build a fort to counter the Dutch--who eventually drove the Portuguese out anyway. Colonialists throughout history seldom had much respect for local cultures and religions. This temple was renowned enough to have been mentioned in famous Indian Hindu religious hymns dating back to the 600s AD. So what you see now on this cliff-edge (it's a 150-metre vertical drop to the ocean), on a stretch of land sticking out into the Indian ocean, is the 1950s-built temple. There are no thousand pillars, but that doesn't take away the reverence in which the Hindus hold this place of worship. It can be very busy, especially on weekends. On top of the usual devotees you can have weddings in progress, which could swell the numbers and cause an unholy crush. This is what I ran into when I visited. As a tourist, you can get pretty close to the temple by car or van and very close by hiring a tuktuk, or auto, as they call the small converted motorbikes that can carry a max of 3 people at a time. There's a narrow road leading up to the top of the rock. There are lots of small shops on both sides of this road. The road could be thronging with people, and, in the middle of all this, you'll have tuktuks trying to wend their way up and down the hill. It can be manic. When you get to about 50 metres from the temple, footwear have to be removed and put away in racks that have been provided in a small shed. After this it will be barefooted trek up some steps and then you'll be in front of the temple. Those who are used to always wearing slippers and shoes could be in for a shock at this stage as the sand and stones underfoot could feel like spikes. If you persevere, you can look around the place--it won't take more than 15 minutes. If you are a devotee or have some interest in this temple's historical significance, you could spend a lot more time here.

Trincomalee, is on the north east side of Sri Lanka and is about 260 kms from Colombo (via Dambulla). It is famous as one of the finest natural deep-water harbours in the world. Trincomalee is home to some of the most picturesque and scenic beaches like Nilaveli, Uppaveli and Pigeon Island which are relatively un-spoilt and clean. In recent times Trincomalee has become popular for whale watching too. Since the beaches have knee-deep shallow waters that runs hundreds of feet into the sea, it affords ample opportunities for surfing, scuba diving, fishing etc. The other attractions that this town has are Trikoneswar temple, the Dutch Fort and the Kanniya hot water springs. •	Trikoneswar temple -  The actual name of this place was Thirukonamalai from which the new name Trincomalee  emerged. Legend from Hindu mythology has it that Goddess Parvathi suddenly desired to have a large palatial mansion, where she could live happily with Shiva and her children Karthikeya and Ganesha. Lord Shiva summoned the architect of the Devas, Vishwakarma to fulfil Parvathi’s desire. He flew southwards and chose a beautiful spot on the island of Lanka. There he raised a magnificent structure, gleaming with gold and gems, cooled with water fountains and filled with the smell of many divine flowers in the garden, a palace that qualified to be the residence of the Mother of the three worlds. Shiva and Shakthi came down to Lanka to find a suitable brahmana for the Grihapravesha where they encountered Ravana performing austere penance invoking Shiva. Pleased Shiva blessed him and Parvati requested Ravana to perform the Grihapravesha. On the prescribed date, Ravana performed the ceremony with much grandeur and splendor, with the correct usage of all the mantras and shlokas. Shiva and Parvathi entered their mansion and added further sanctity to the spot. Parvathi was extremely pleased with Ravana’s prowess in the Vedas and offered him any boon that he wanted as dakshina for performing the ceremonies. The shrewd man that he was, he instead asked the house for himself. Left with no choice she agreed. Ravana then built a gigantic temple with thousand pillars, replete with architectural details, dedicated to the goddess Shankari Devi. The temple was located on the top a cliff that fell sharply into the magnificent sea below. However much of the temple was destroyed during the Portuguese invasion who plundered the temple.  Later the Dutch used the pillars to built a fort nearby.  The present temple is of much modest dimensions compared to the one of yore. Koneswaram has shrines to Ganesha, Subramanya and other Shivite deities. The recently recovered Panchaloha idols are worshipped in the Vasantha Mandapam. There is a separate smaller temple dedicated to the goddess worshipped as Mathumai Ambal. The temple offers a spectacular view of the calm Indian ocean stretching out for miles. By the edge of the cliff, stands an ancient Bilva tree, under which Sri Rama is said to have meditated. •	A must visit is the Pigeon Island, a little wildlife sanctuary where the blue Rock pigeons breed, and whose waters around are a paradise of colorful fishes. The beach swarms with crabs of various sizes. Ideal for snorkeling and swimming in the shallow pristine waters, the island can be reached by boats hired from any of the hotels or from the beach. •	The seven hot springs of Kanniyayi, is another must to visit. Again legend has it that Ravana’s mother’s last rites were performed at the Kanniya Hot Springs. The waters are mildly hot and people believe that bathing in these wells will refresh them. All in all a beautiful place with lots of fond memories to cherish.

Koneswaram temple of Trincomalee is a classical-medieval Hindu temple complex in Trincomalee. Built significantly during the reign of the early Cholas and the Five Dravidians of the Early Pandyan Kingdom atop Konesar Malai, a promontory overlooking Trincomalee District, Gokarna bay and the Indian Ocean. The monument contains its main shrine to Shiva in the form Kona-Eiswara, shortened to Konesar and is a major place for Hindu pilgrimage.  Annually Koneswaram Temple has their Thiruvilah festival. The construction time of Koneswaram has been estimated by comparison between carved reliefs on the temple's ruins, literature on the shrine and the inscriptions commonly used in royal charters from the 5th to 18th centuries. Koneswaram was likely founded before 400 BCE although its exact date of birth remains vague.

My first time at Konneswaran temple located on the cliff of Trincomalee, and it was absolutely marvelous. It is an immensely holy place, first established around 205 B.C. We visited during a ceremony and stopped to watch a while. My children had never been, so it was a wonderful introduction to a part of Hindu culture, something they would not experience from reading a book. The stunning statue of Lord Shiva, to whom the temple is dedicated, rises above the hill and it is almost as if he protects everyone, human and animal in the vicinity. The aura is powerful. The king was known to worship Shiva. The water is azure blue, the best time to visit is when  the sun is slowly making its descent, it is a stunning vista at 5pm. It is important to gauge the weather during the season in Trincomalee because it is hot between noon and 4pm. There are some colorful stalls on your walk to the temple. Koneswaram Temple or also known as Thriu Koneswaram Temple is located on Swami rock adjacent to the Indian Ocean in Trincomalee, Sri Lanka. The temple is under renovation now.  Paintings of the Idols are taking places during our visit to this temple in January 2015.. Thiru Koneswaram Temple is dedicated to Lord Siva. This is called as " Dakshina- Kailasam" and is a classical-medieval Hindu temple complex in Trincomalee,  This is more a Hindu Religious pilgrimage centre in Sri Lanka. The temple has a huge complex housing the deities of  Bhadrakali, Ganesha, Vishnu Thirumal, Surya, Raavana, Ambal-Shakti, Murugan and Shiva who presides at the promontory’s height. As we enter from the right side of the temple, we find the Statue of Ravana and opposite to Ravana statue is "Sivaling". As we further enter in to the temple, we can see Lord Ganesha, Lord Muruga and the Shrine of Lord Siva. There is the Goddess of "Shankari Devi", one of the 18 Shakti Peetams. Many people of this area are not aware that this is the Shakti Peeth:'Shankari Devi" located at Koneswaram Temple. I am of the opinion that the name Trincomalee is perhaps derived from :"Thirukonamalai Konesar" ( a Tamil Word). The journey for pilgrims in the town begins at the opening of Konesar Road and follows a path to the temple. Autos ply from the Konesar Road up to the temple. The view of the Indian Ocean from the temple is beautiful. At the entrance of the temple, a huge Idol of Lord Siva is constructed giving a valiant look. It is one of the must visit temple in Sri Lanka and particularlu for those who come from India. We are happy we could visit this temple and enjoy the temple and view surrounding the temple premises.

This Hindu kovil has a history going beyond recorded history. It is the second most important Hindu temple in Sri Lanka devoted to the Lord Shiva, after Munneswaram. The original form of the kovil was destroyed, ransacked and pilfered by the Portuguese (who displayed their best abilities in the task) in the 1500s. The current structure is a modern construct. However legend has it that it that there has stood a Shiva temple here since prehistory. It is referenced in the Ramayanaya (2000BCE) and the Mahabarathe epics (400-100BCE), The temple was built by the Sinhala King Maha Ravana of Lanka, the greatest human devotee of the Lord Shiva.

After passing a series of shops selling refreshments, souvenirs and devotionals you get to the point where you hand over your shoes and continue barefoot. This is also the right moment to cover your shoulders and your knees. Approaching the temple you notice the big golden statue of Koneshwaran. On top of the steep promontory which is one of the outer corners of "the best natural harbour in the world" and steeped in history the Koneswaram Temple is the must- see attraction in Trincomalee. There are of course the ubiquitous tuk tuks, but if you have the energy, walk up to it - through historical Fort Frederick, held by the Portuguese, the Dutch, the French and the English; with its monumental main entrance, its shadowed alleys and collossal banyan trees, its quirky English bungalows and "Army welfare cafes", its broadly- smiling soldiers and its population of half- tame deer the walk leads you through one of the most picturesque army barracks I have seen. Then, through an alleyway of stalls selling offerings and religious paraphernalia, the drink you absolutely need and the souvenir fridge magnet you probably don't need you advance to the magnificent statue of Vishnu and the temple itself which was so important during the Ages of European expansion into the Indian Ocean and beyond that the zealous Portuguese chose to destroy it. My husband and I are spiritual but not Hindu. Nevertheless we felt at awe at the temple which today enshrines Hindu relics which survived the Portuguese onslaught. Outside you may be charmed or disgusted by macaque monkeys munching at the fruit offerings, and you will definitely enjoy the ocean views all the way across the outer harbour and to the lighthouse on the southern shore. A (very safe) walk on the edge of the cliff is not for the faint- hearted because of these views! In the blue or green waters right below the promontory you could snorkel or dive for temple ruins or Dutch cannons. (see my review Sri Lanka Diving Tours). A half day excursion you will not want to miss.

We went to the Pigeon Island which is one of the best for snorkelling and swimming. You can hire a boat and do a day or half day trip. We also went to the first Buddhist Stupa built in Sri Lanka which is little known and it was a lovely trip. It is called Girigadu Seya and is about an hours drive from Trincomalee. Suggest that visitors go there towards dusk as there is a homage (pooja) conducted by army and navy personnel which is beautiful. There are a few hundred steps to climb but the view and the history behind is worthwhile the trek. We also visited Marble Beach and had an excellent lunch at the café. The Koneswaram Temple is atop a hill that juts out into the ocean. It commands a wide view of the town, the harbour, and islands in the waters beyond. I teamed with a fellow traveller and borrowed a pair of push-bikes to roam around town. To access the hill, you have to enter the Fort which is a Sri Lankan Army outpost now. The last few metres is perhaps too steep to cycle up. So one needs to walk it up, dragging the cycle. Once you reach there, the view is worth the huff and puff (apart from the temple for the devout, of course).

This is a nice temple to visit to get a taste of Hindu culture and art. The location is wonderful with a great view of the sea. The little walk to the temple through street vendors were wonderful where you can buy various food and handicraft unique to this area.

This isn't the most extravagant temple in Sri Lanka by any stretch, but it is very much worth a visit as a break from the beach. It's at the top of a hill inside the Fort, so has a great view back to the town and out to sea. Like most Hindu temples, it has a lot of very gaudy ornamentation, though not as over the top as some. As of oct 2012 parts of it are under repair which detracts from the visit. A tuk tuk can take you most of the way up but you'll have to walk the last couple of hundred meters. You'll run a gauntlet of vendors. They are actually half the fun. Stop and check out their snacks and wares. Try the lime juice or a tea. The people will be very friendly and guide you along. Some outdated guide books say that the Fort is still closed off by the military and you'll need to surrender your passport. That's no longer true. There is still an army base in the Fort, but access to the park and temple is no issue. You'll have to take your shoes off for about the last 100 meters. The pavement can be hot, very HOT. Even the locals were screaming and running for spots the sun wasn't hitting. Visiting early in the morning would probably solve that. Like all temples of all denominations in Sri Lanka, they welcome people of other faiths, but be sure to dress modestly. Cover your shoulders and avoid short shorts. Ideally your knees at least should be covered. That applies to both sexes. Avoid taking flash photographs and interrupting or distracting people while they are worshipping and you will be welcome.

There probably should be a sign up for tourists just to tell them how to behave, where to go, and what to do at Hindu temples. I was not sure if we were allowed inside and so just walked around the outside, although apparently it would have been fine to enter. I didn't want to cause offence and didn't want to disturb worshippers with questions. This said, the temple is striking and in a beautiful setting on the edge of the rock, definitely worth a visit combined with the fort.
